findings.trigger_condition: Processing graphs with many unhashable nodes
findings.root_cause: O(N squared) lookup complexity for unhashable nodes. For every unhashable node lookup, the code scans ALL previously registered unhashable nodes (O(U)) and then ALL registered hashable nodes (O(H)). With N total nodes, this gives O(N squared) overall complexity for building the graph when unhashable nodes are common.
findings.impact: Severe performance degradation with large graphs. A graph with 1000 unhashable nodes would require approximately 500,000 equality comparisons just for node registration. For graphs with 10,000+ nodes, this becomes intractable.
findings.suggested_validation: Benchmark with chains of 100, 200, 400 unhashable nodes and measure the time ratio. O(N squared) will show ~4x time when doubling N.

findings.trigger_condition: Processing graphs with any mix of hashable and unhashable nodes
findings.root_cause: Even hashable node lookups pay O(U) cost to cross-check against all unhashable nodes. The code iterates through every registered unhashable node for every hashable lookup to handle the case where a hashable value might compare equal to an unhashable one. This means even graphs with mostly hashable nodes pay the O(U) penalty if any unhashable nodes exist.
findings.impact: Performance degradation for mixed hashable/unhashable graphs. Even when 99 percent of nodes are hashable, the 1 percent unhashable nodes force every lookup to scan the full unhashable list.
findings.suggested_validation: Benchmark with 100 hashable nodes vs 100 hashable + 100 unhashable nodes. The mixed case will be significantly slower even for hashable lookups.

findings.trigger_condition: Uncommon but theoretically possible: hashable_ids populated in non-ID order
findings.root_cause: When looking up an unhashable value and scanning hashable_ids, the code breaks after the first matching node, relying on hashable_ids being in strictly increasing ID order to find the earliest match. While the current implementation does append in ID order (preserving the invariant), this is a fragile dependency that could break if the list population logic changes.
findings.impact: Low risk under current implementation, but represents a latent correctness hazard from tight coupling between the lookup algorithm and list population order. Future refactoring could break earliest-match semantics.
findings.suggested_validation: Verify that hashable_ids and unhashable_ids are always appended in strictly increasing node_id order. Audit any future changes to node registration that could violate this.
